concept.name: Backwardation
concept.definition: A market situation in which futures prices are progressively lower in the more distant delivery months than in the nearer months or spot, i.e. the futures curve slopes downward. It is the opposite of contango and often signals tight near-term supply or a high convenience yield on holding the physical commodity.
concept.intuition: Buyers pay a premium to get the commodity now rather than later — immediacy is worth more than future delivery.
concept.mechanics: Measured by comparing contract months: F(t, T2) < F(t, T1) for T2 > T1. Backwardation arises when the benefit of owning the physical material (convenience yield, e.g. keeping a production process running) exceeds storage and financing costs; the CFTC glossary illustrates it as a January gold quote of $360 versus $355 for June.
concept.formula: Backwardation condition: F(t, T2) < F(t, T1) for T2 > T1; calendar spread F(t, T2) - F(t, T1) < 0.
concept.failure_modes: Backwardation rewards long futures positions via positive roll yield only if the curve shape persists; a sudden supply normalization can flip the curve to contango and erase the roll advantage. Near-dated spikes can make the measured backwardation exaggerated relative to deferred months.
concept.misconceptions: Backwardation is not necessarily a sign that prices are about to fall; it is a statement about relative prices across delivery months. It is also not 'abnormal' in any regulatory sense — it is a standard response to scarcity.
concept.example: If the WTI front month trades at $85 while the contract six months out trades at $81, the market is backwardated by $4, typical of a tight, undersupplied crude market.

citations.source: CFTC Futures Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
CME Group, CME Institute: What is Contango and Backwardation
